themes.theme: Reporting from national authorities and Member States to the Commission
themes.definition: Periodic reports and notifications that Member States, national authorities and the EDPS owe the Commission, the AI Office and the Board.
themes.what_is_set_out: Member States report to the Commission every two years from 2 August 2025 on the financial and human resources of national competent authorities, with an assessment of their adequacy (Art. 70(6)), and annually on fines issued and related litigation (Art. 99(11)); they notify their penalty rules (Recital 179) and their national laws on police biometric identification within 30 days of adoption (EU043). Market surveillance authorities report annually to the Commission on prohibited practices that occurred and the measures taken (Art. 74(2)); together with data protection authorities they report annually on real-time biometric identification use on a Commission template, with the EDPS reporting for Union bodies, and the EDPS also notifies the Commission annually of the fines it has imposed. National competent authorities running sandboxes report annually to the AI Office and the Board, and notifying authorities report their findings on changes to a notified body's designation to the Commission and other Member States within three months. No passage states a consequence for failing to report, and EU043 notes that notifying a national law 'does not provide a presumption of conformity' with the AI Act.
themes.holders: Member States; market surveillance authorities; national data protection authorities; the EDPS; national competent authorities; notifying authorities.
themes.binding: Statutory duties ('shall'); recitals use 'should'. Consequences are not stated; EU043 records a 30-day deadline for notifying national laws.

quotes.quote: By 2 August 2025, and once every two years thereafter, Member States shall report to the Commission on the status of the financial and human resources of the national competent authorities, with an assessment of their adequacy.
They shall also annually report to the Commission about the use of prohibited practices that occurred during that year and about the measures taken.

Member States shall, on an annual basis, report to the Commission about the administrative fines they have issued during that year, in accordance with this Article, and about any related litigation or judicial proceedings.
must submit annual reports on such use to the Commission. These reports shall be made on the basis of a template provided by the Commission.

themes.theme: Commission answerable to the European Parliament and Council
themes.definition: Controls through which the Commission answers to the co-legislators for its delegated acts and for evaluating the AI Act and its enforcement.
themes.what_is_set_out: The European Parliament or the Council may revoke the Commission's delegated powers 'at any time', and a delegated act enters into force only if neither objects within three months (Art. 97(3), (6)); the Omnibus applies this to its new delegated powers, with a Commission report on the delegation before the period ends. The Commission must assess once a year whether to amend Annex III and the list of prohibited practices (Art. 112(1)), and by 2 August 2028 and every four years evaluate and report to Parliament and Council on the Annex III area headings, the Art. 50 transparency list and amendments to strengthen supervision and governance (Art. 112(2); Recital 174). Its reports must assess 'the structure of enforcement and the possible need for a Union agency' (Art. 112(3)) and, by 2 August 2028, whether the AI Office has 'sufficient powers and competences' and enough resources (Art. 112(5)); the reports are made public.
themes.holders: The Commission (answers); the European Parliament and the Council.
themes.binding: Statutory. Consequences: revocation ends the delegation, and an objection stops a delegated act entering into force. For the review clauses no consequence is stated beyond possible amendment proposals.

quotes.quote: shall enter into force only if no objection has been expressed by either the European Parliament or the Council within a period of three months of notification

By 2 August 2028, the Commission shall evaluate the functioning of the AI Office, whether the AI Office has been given sufficient powers and competences to fulfil its tasks

themes.definition: Provisions naming the authority to which providers and deployers, including public bodies, answer for AI Act compliance.
themes.what_is_set_out: National market surveillance authorities designated by Member States enforce the AI Act, including the prohibitions, with all the powers of Regulation 2019/1020 (Recital 156; EU043 para 53; EU_Art50 para 151), and national competent authorities 'should exercise their powers independently, impartially and without bias' (Recital 154). For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies the EDPS is the competent and market surveillance authority, except for the Court of Justice acting in its judicial capacity (Art. 70(9), 74(9), 3(48)). The AI Office has powers to monitor and supervise AI systems built on a general-purpose model where model and system come from the same provider (Art. 75(1)), which the Omnibus spells out as 'all the powers of a market surveillance authority'. Authorities supervising biometric systems used for law enforcement, migration, asylum, border control or the administration of justice 'should have effective investigative and corrective powers', including access to all personal data processed (Recital 159); financial supervisors are designated for AI used by regulated financial institutions, which is marginal for public bodies; and under the Omnibus the national competent authority supervises testing under the new Art. 60a. [inference] For a national public body using AI the answerable relationship is with its national market surveillance authority, for a Union body with the EDPS, and for a public body using an assistant built by a model provider possibly with the AI Office.
themes.holders: National market surveillance authorities; national competent authorities; the EDPS; the AI Office; financial supervisory authorities; providers and deployers (answer to them), including Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies.
themes.binding: Statutory designations and powers in the Articles; recitals use 'should'; EU043 and EU_Art50 restate the designations. Consequences flow from the enforcement and fines provisions.

themes.theme: Investigation, evaluation and corrective powers over AI systems
themes.definition: Supervisors' powers to evaluate an AI system, check a provider's classification, inspect, demand access and explanations, and order correction, restriction or withdrawal.
themes.what_is_set_out: Where a market surveillance authority has 'sufficient reason' to consider that a system presents a risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, it must evaluate the system against all AI Act requirements and can require corrective action, withdrawal or recall (Art. 79(2)); where it suspects a provider wrongly classed a system as not high-risk, it evaluates the system, requires compliance, and fines for not correcting it or for deliberate misclassification (Art. 80). It may run checks using the EU database (Art. 80(8)), act on formal findings such as a missing CE marking, declaration or registration by requiring an end to the non-compliance and then restricting or prohibiting the system (Art. 83), exercise some powers remotely, and use a 'specific safeguard procedure' for systems presenting risks (Recital 157). Recital 159 says authorities supervising biometric systems in law enforcement, migration, border control or justice should have effective investigative and corrective powers. The Omnibus gives the AI Office, for systems in its competence, powers to act on its own initiative or on a complaint, request information by simple request or by binding decision, carry out 'all necessary remote or on-site inspections', 'order operators to provide access to, and explanations relating to, their AI systems', make operators' commitments binding, adopt non-compliance decisions with fines, and require operators to report the measures they took; it must tell a national single point of contact within four months whether it will use its powers on a request, or why not. [inference] These are the cell's main external checks on AI systems, and every one is triggered by suspicion, complaint or discretion rather than by a routine schedule.
themes.holders: Market surveillance authorities; the AI Office; providers and other operators (answer to them).
themes.binding: Statutory powers and duties. Consequences: corrective action, withdrawal, recall, restriction or prohibition; fines (Art. 80(4), (7); Art. 99); under the Omnibus, binding commitments, non-compliance decisions, fines and periodic penalty payments, and costs of supervision reclaimable for non-compliance (per the coder note).

themes.theme: Commission and AI Office oversight of general-purpose AI models
themes.definition: The powers by which the AI Office and the Commission monitor general-purpose model providers, request documentation and model access, run evaluations and impose measures.
themes.what_is_set_out: The AI Office 'may take the necessary actions to monitor' general-purpose model providers' compliance, including their adherence to approved codes of practice (Art. 89(1)). The Commission may request documentation or additional information, which the provider must supply, with fines for incorrect or misleading answers (Art. 91), and after consulting the Board the AI Office may evaluate a model where that information is insufficient or to investigate systemic risks, especially after a qualified alert (Art. 92(1)); for this it may request access 'through APIs or further appropriate technical means and tools, including source code' (Art. 92(3)). It may then request measures including risk mitigation, restriction, withdrawal or recall, and impose fines of up to 3% of global turnover or EUR 15 million (Recital 164; EU088 para 103). The AI Office monitors providers' copyright policy and training summaries 'without verifying or proceeding to a work-by-work assessment' of the training data (Recital 108). EU088 says providers already training models in August 2025 should tell the AI Office proactively how and when they will comply, with fines enforced from 2 August 2026.
themes.holders: The AI Office and the Commission (enforcers); providers of general-purpose AI models (answer); the Board (consulted).
themes.binding: Statutory powers ('may') and provider duties ('shall supply'); fines under Art. 101; recitals use 'should'; EU088 states non-binding expectations and a transitional enforcement date.
themes.checks: Model evaluations (Art. 92): trigger: insufficient information under Art. 91, or investigation of systemic risks, especially after a qualified alert; compared against: not stated in these passages; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the AI Office, after consulting the Board; what happens with the result: may lead to requested measures (mitigation, restriction, withdrawal, recall) and fines. Copyright monitoring: no work-by-work check of training data.

themes.theme: Data protection supervisors' review of AI models
themes.definition: How data protection supervisory authorities (national authorities and the EDPS) are to review controllers' AI models, the corrective measures open to them, and the prior consultation route.
themes.what_is_set_out: The EDPB Opinion (EU074) tells supervisory authorities to evaluate case by case whether a controller's measures to make an AI model anonymous are 'appropriate and effective'; if they cannot confirm this, they may find the controller 'has failed to meet its accountability obligations under Article 5(2) GDPR'. Authorities should also verify that controllers relying on legitimate interest documented the three cumulative conditions, expect detail on the model's type, functions and deployment context, consider whether the deployer published its balancing test, and assess the lawfulness of both the developer and the controller that acquired the model, taking into account whether the deployer 'conducted an appropriate assessment' of how the model was developed. On a finding of infringement they may order remediation, issue fines, limit processing temporarily, or order erasure of part of the dataset or of the model itself. Under the EUDPR an EU institution that cannot mitigate risks by reasonable means must consult the EDPS beforehand (EDPS_AI_risk), and the EDPS orientations lower this threshold: if controllers are 'not sure' after the impact assessment whether risks are mitigated, they should consult. [inference] This is the cell's most developed regime for scrutinising a deployer's due diligence on a model it acquired from someone else.
themes.holders: National supervisory authorities and the EDPS; controllers that develop or deploy AI models; EUIs.
themes.binding: The EDPB Opinion is non-binding interpretation addressed to supervisory authorities; the corrective powers it describes are statutory ('may'); prior consultation is a statutory duty (Art. 40(1) EUDPR) restated, and the lower EDPS threshold is a recommendation ('should proceed').
themes.checks: Anonymity review: trigger: a supervisory authority's investigation, case by case; compared against: whether the controller's measures to make the model anonymous are 'appropriate and effective'; metric or threshold: not stated; who: the supervisory authority; what happens with the result: possible finding of failed accountability and corrective measures. Deployer's assessment of an acquired model: trigger: deployment; compared against: the lawfulness of the model's development; metric: not stated; who: the deploying controller, reviewed by the supervisory authority; result: a factor in the authority's assessment. Prior consultation: trigger: residual risk after the impact assessment; who: the EDPS; result: not stated.

quotes.quote: SAs should evaluate, on a case -by-case basis, if the measures implemented by the controller to ensure and prove that an AI model is anonymous are appropriate and effective.

themes.definition: Rules that hold the conformity assessment bodies that check high-risk AI systems to account, and their audits of providers.
themes.what_is_set_out: Conformity assessment bodies apply for notification to the notifying authority of their Member State (Art. 29), must update their documentation 'whenever relevant changes occur' so that authority can monitor continuous compliance (Omnibus), and must report certificates issued and any refusal, restriction, suspension or withdrawal (Art. 45). They take 'full responsibility' for subcontractors and subsidiaries, publish a list of subsidiaries, hold liability insurance for their assessments, and hand the notifying authority all documentation, including providers' documentation, on request. If a notified body no longer meets the Art. 31 requirements or fails its obligations, the notifying authority 'shall restrict, suspend or withdraw the designation' and reports to the Commission and Member States within three months; the Commission investigates doubts about competence (Art. 37) and, under the Omnibus, may withdraw tasks it delegated 'with immediate effect' if they are not performed 'adequately', a term left undefined. 'An appeal procedure against decisions of the notified bodies' shall be available (Art. 44(3)), but who runs it and who may appeal are not stated. Notified bodies in turn carry out periodic audits of providers' quality management systems and give the provider an audit report (Annex VII 5.3).
themes.holders: Conformity assessment bodies and notified bodies; notifying authorities; the Commission; providers (audited).
themes.binding: Statutory. Consequences: restriction, suspension or withdrawal of designation; withdrawal of delegated tasks; notified-body obligations under Arts 31, 33 and 34 are fineable under Art. 99(4)(f); a body cannot be notified without applying [inference].

themes.theme: Procedural safeguards on supervisors and challenge routes for operators
themes.definition: Limits on how supervisors use their powers, and routes by which providers and other operators can challenge supervisory decisions.
themes.what_is_set_out: A market surveillance authority's decision or objection on real-world testing must give grounds and say how the provider can challenge it (Art. 76(4)); fines are subject to 'effective judicial remedies and due process' (Art. 99(10)); Union bodies facing EDPS proceedings must be heard (Art. 100(4)); and all Commission decisions are reviewable by the Court of Justice, which has unlimited jurisdiction over fines on general-purpose model providers (Art. 101(5), Recital 169) and, under the Omnibus, over AI Office fines and penalty payments. Operators under AI Office investigation have rights of defence and of access to the file, information requests must state the right to Court review, and where national law requires it a national judge checks that coercive inspection measures are 'neither arbitrary nor excessive'. Authorities must keep information confidential, protecting intellectual property and trade secrets including source code (Art. 78; EU088 para 105), and market surveillance must not interfere with judges acting in their judicial capacity (Art. 74(8)). Scientific panel experts publish declarations of interests, and general-purpose model providers have the procedural rights in Art. 18 of Regulation 2019/1020. These routes protect operators against regulators; routes for affected people appear in the complaint, explanation and data-subject-rights themes. [inference] Confidentiality limits what regulators can publish about AI systems that public bodies use.
themes.holders: Market surveillance authorities, the EDPS, the Commission and the AI Office (bound by the safeguards); the Court of Justice and national judicial authorities (review); providers, operators and Union bodies under investigation (protected); scientific panel experts.
themes.binding: Statutory; recitals restate Treaty law. The consequence of breaching a safeguard is review by the courts (cancel, reduce or increase fines).
